en: When we reach the middle of the road,
I shall slaughter him as a sacrifice.
Upon Beijing of Kakan-Chin,
Thus shall I take my vengeance!”
All the champions made ready,
All the warriors made ready;
At that time the Muslims
Found a task to occupy them.
Hero Bakai, that saintly elder,
Put on his blue lynx-fur cap,
Wielded his mottled blue shield.
Of a saddle-shaped ridge,
He climbed the crest and looked;
Dust rose in surges and surges.
When he looked at the surging dust,
Khan Bakai was beside himself.
The many Chinese, in utter turmoil,
Had crowded together.
For the infidels to rejoice,
Their day had dawned;
When your champion Alake fell to a bullet,
The infidels had bound him upon a mule.
“Here is your fugitive!” they would say,
Before Karykan;
To carry the glad news, the infidels
Had loaded the hero and set out.
Then they beat their drums,
Now they played their flutes;
An immense idol, big as a house,
Had they not made it of bronze?
The infidels tied it up high.
Girded with a gray pouch-belt,
When he saw the Chinese array,
That peerless leopard
Now cried out, “Islam!”
Making Buurul prance,
Making whoever he met crawl,
Finding the means to best them,
Your hero smashed them all;
Upon six vast Chinese hosts,
He fell with a shout of slaughter.
Noble Bakai, Ajybai,
And your generous Manas—there were three;
In the desert of It-Ölbös,
They wrested back your Alake's body.
Then, with golden forelock and tasseled belt,
Azizkan's only son,
Your generous Manas held before him,
Pressed his cheek against his cheek.
Without ceasing his low moan,
Manas cried aloud and began his words:
“My pair of twin lambs,
Having devoured both alike,
How can I go on without longing?
Having let Akkula fall to a bullet,
Having sent Almambet to martyrdom,
With my wings broken,
Parted from Khan Chubak,
How can I return to Talas?!
Almambet—my good fortune when sent into battle;
My Chubak—my vast army when he followed behind.
A pine alone, utterly alone,
Parted from my leopard,
I, grieving Manas, am alone.
A hawthorn alone, all alone,
Parted from my band of companions,
I, desolate Manas, am alone!
The pea-shrub upon the hill—
My fortunate Almam, take me with you!
My Alake, my crag no goose could circle,
My impregnable black mountain,
I was steel that cut through stone;
Now I find myself bound fast.
Having devoured my champions,
I find myself stricken blind!
When I move, my feet cannot step;
I have become like a snake.
Parted from my twins,
With no mane or tail at all,
I have become like a wild ass.
My Alake, my gift from China,
My Chubake, my hero from the Oygut,
My boundless river has dried;
My people, I stand powerless.
I let Beijing take them;
My people, what can I do!
A broad river, a boundless lake,
My Chubak, my meadowsweet valley;
Given for my fortune by the Creator,
Almambet, my hero who came into my hands.
Yesterday, in the hollow of Zhylgyndy,
Along broad Talas,
I would slice and eat horse rump.
If hardship fell upon this head,
With your Alma standing, roaring,
I would say, ‘I shall overthrow the governor-general.’
Has the governor-general found peace?
When seven vast dark enemy hosts came,
Entering with his coat thrown over his shoulders, he attacked—
Has my Alake's back been broken!
Having devoured my champions,
O God, has my life now found peace!
Girded at the waist with a white pouch-belt,
When sixty thousand warriors came,
He entered and attacked alone.
I have let a bad name fall upon me;
My precious Almam, take me with you!”
Yesterday, Manas, the leopard,
When he turned Taybuurul's head,
As he stood exhausted with grief,
Almambet's Sarala,
Tossing his forelock to the sky,
The black steel bit
Clattering in his throat,
His tail like a strand of silk
Lashing between his hind legs,
Had no tongue with which to speak.
That creature, wiser than other beasts,
Lowered his head to the ground;
That blessed beast had grown straight and lean;
He had taken up mourning.
The reason for his mourning:
They united when tiny as lice,
Joined when thumb-sized,
Chased one another when he was a foal.
Though Sarala was a beast,
That creature and your Alake,
The two were born on the very same day.
Then Almambet's Sarala,
Upon a saddle-shaped hollow,
Was standing still.
Your renowned Alma—
Though Sarala was a beast,
He had no tongue with which to speak;
Your noble, renowned Alma
He was mourning.
He had lowered his head to the ground,
Not clipping grass with a crunch,
Not swallowing water with a gulp;
The noble beast had grown lean and fit;
He had taken up mourning.
The lion Bakai and hero Manas,
Your Almake's Sarala,
Caught him at a distance.
When the sovereign prince Bakai
Turned Sarala's head,
Khan Manas's forty companions,
Beside sovereign Manas,
As they loaded Almambet upon Sarala,
The fine rope made of silk,
Then saintly Bakai, the dear lion,
Wound and folded twelve times;
Their saintly Almambet,
Oh hero, he loaded upon Sarala.
Your elder Bakai, the leopard,
Who found words at an unexpected moment,
Who found eyes in a dark place,
Bound him again, fastening him close.
To the saddle-thong itself,
The ingot made of gold,
He tied it again, fastening it close:
“The champion Khan Almambet—
When the Muslims reach and bury him,
Let this be their payment,” he said;
Good heavens, he entrusted it to the saddle-thong.
Grasping him at the waist, he folded him;
Your blue-maned champion Alma,
He loaded upon Sarala.
As they loaded your Alake upon Sarala,
The honored men wept, the khans wept,
All the multitude of people wept,
The heroes Ajybai and Bakai wept,
Your generous lion Manas wept.
Khan Bakai held Sarala
By the bit, sobbing;
The handful of Muslims,
With turmoil fallen upon their heads,
Then stood weeping and wailing.
When all his recourse failed him,
His sworn companion, Khan Bakai,
Held Sarala close by the bit.
As though he could understand speech,
Almambet's body
He entrusted to him as a solemn charge:
“My dear Sarala,
Lower your head to the ground;
Almambet's body,
Let them see it safe and sound;
Noble beast, carry it to the Muslims!
If you do not carry it to the Muslims,
I shall know how bestial you are.
Calling you a beast among beasts,
I shall liken you to a donkey.
Ah, my dear Sarala,
At Beijing that the Holy One could not touch,
We have let a bad name fall upon us.
Of mankind, the lone lion Alma
Is entrusted to you alone!
Bring him back to me;
My dear Sarala,
Let my own eyes see him!”
Grasping his forelock, he could only kiss him;
“Farewell, Sarala,” he said, kissing him.
Your elder Bakai, the lion,
The swift steed Sarala,
Then drove him onto the road.
Your generous Manas, the leopard,
Leaning upon his battle-axe,
Was left lamenting his precious one.
His dear eyes like a saker's,
With each turn, tears flowed;
His dear eyes like currants,
Tears flowed a whip's length.
Your hero returned from entering Beijing,
Your hero was parted from his champions,
Had let all his people be slaughtered.
He took turmoil away from Beijing.
Karabayyr battle steeds,
With sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs—
Swift steeds he took from Beijing.
All the precious treasures,
He bundled and took from Beijing.
Gold and silver,
He loaded and took from Beijing.
Noble young wives and beautiful girls,
He plundered and took from Beijing.
He took red-tailed elephants;
He loaded gold upon elephants and took it;
He took a thousand dark-eyed women.
The most able warriors,
Those returning safely from Beijing,
The accomplished champions,
Took seven thousand horses each;
The lesser men who could not match them
Took seven hundred horses each.
All the exceptional ones
Drove six thousand horses each;
The lesser men who guarded their lives
Drove six hundred horses each.
All the mighty ones
Took girls in red dresses, slender-waisted,
Girls who moved with graceful swaying.
All the valued ones
Took skilled women with thimbles;
They took gold and jewels by the pood.
Opening the way for Islam,
Scattering the Chinese herds,
Plundering their goods,
Wreaking such destruction,
All their champions slaughtered,
Those left alive among the dead
Dispersed toward their destinations.
Those who dwelt in Sary-Arka,
Whom all the people who saw them
Called weighty, formidable warriors,
Who hulled their millet clean as stone,
